query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The high-entropy alloy, initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service due to the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds, such as Laves phases, which reduce the ductility of the alloy.
generation.boundary: service temperature, loading rate, and stress intensity
generation.uncertainty: the exact mechanism of brittle intermetallic compound formation and its effect on ductility

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if no significant change in toughness or fracture behavior is observed under varying loading conditions and service environments, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). For HEAs to reach their full potential, it is essential to predict the phases that ultimately form. Wang et al. studied the microstructure and mechanical properties of as-cast and as-annealed CoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloys and found that a high strain hardening rate is observed due to the high density of dislocation tangles surrounding the μ-phase precipitates, resulting in significant strength improvement. Stepanov et al. studied the effect of vanadium content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the CoCrFeMnNiVx high-entropy alloys and found that V content in the alloy system results in the emergence and growth of the σ phase, which results in a noticeable drop in ductility.
